the report be approved.

Resources and the Monitoring Officer to:

Policy 2026

content:
To move
to the formal stages, the Council must agree with the Government
our place in their national phasing. The Council wants to progress
early in 2026 and it would be helpful to have a resolution to that
effect.  However, that will rely upon on
regulations yet to be published. This report will also be an
opportunity to report on further iterations of scenario testing
from September 2025 and any subsequent consultation although the
timing of this report is dependent on dialogue with the Government
and whether regulations are published as anticipated.






DECISION:

 

RESOLVED:

 
1. 
That authority be delegated to the Service Director
for Planning and Housing to publish the notices and timetables
required, as set out in Appendix 1 to the report, to initiate the
formal stages of work on a Local Plan for Cornwall.
2. 
That authority be delegated to the Service Director
for Planning and Housing to respond to the Government consultation
on Spatial Development Strategy geographies to set out the
Council’s wish to prepare one for Cornwall specifically,
consistent with our intended Foundation Strategic Authority
status.
3. 
That authority be delegated to the Service Director
for Planning and Housing to commence any necessary work (including
publication of notices or timetables, as set out in Appendix 1 to
the report, unless otherwise directed by the Cabinet) relating to
the preparation of a Spatial Development Strategy for Cornwall,
using a common evidence base with the Local Plan and seeking to
align the associated timetables, subject to any relevant enabling
regulations.
4. 
That, in respect of recommendation 3 above, the
Council confirms its intent to act as the Strategic Planning
Authority for Cornwall, subject to the relevant enabling
legislation.
5. 
Notwithstanding recommendations 1 to 4 above, that
the Council confirms its intent to properly and fully work in
co-operation with neighbouring authorities on matters of shared
interest, including but not limited to those informed by relevant
travel to work areas, education and health facilities that relate
specifically to the east of Cornwall and key rail, road and ferry
links, as well as acknowledging the key role of the strategic route
to the Isles of Scilly and associated links to further
education.
6. 
That the first report on community engagement work,
as set out at Appendix 2 to the report, be accepted as a key
reference point for further developing the vision, principles and
themes for the Spatial Development Strategy and Local
Plan.
7. 
That a further £1.200m from the Place &
Green Growth reserve be approved to support the programme costs
which are in addition to the previously approved reserve funding of
£2.540m.

 





 

Reason for the Decision: 
 
As
contained within the report.

None
other than contained within the report.

None.

decision_maker: Cabinet
purpose:
The
report sets out the opportunities and implications of Cornwall
becoming a Single Foundation Strategic Authority. This follows from
the letter the Leader received on 26 November 2025 stating that in
“recognition of Cornwall's distinct local identity and
history of programme delivery across the Cornwall footprint, the
Government is minded, on an exceptional basis, to work with you to
explore designating the council as a Single Foundation Strategic
Authority”. Furthermore, on 12 February 2026, the
consultation on Spatial Development Strategies (SDS) and footprints
was published (separate paper) and the Minister for Devolution
wrote to Chief Executives to say that “the development of SDS
footprints is also an opportunity to agree the shape of devolution
geographies for areas currently without a Strategic
Authority”. Areas in England have been invited to submit an
expression of interest by 20 March 2026.
content:
The
report sets out the opportunities and implications of Cornwall
becoming a Single Foundation Strategic Authority. This follows from
the letter the Leader received on 26 November 2025 stating that in
“recognition of Cornwall's distinct local identity and
history of programme delivery across the Cornwall footprint, the
Government is minded, on an exceptional basis, to work with you to
explore designating the council as a Single Foundation Strategic
Authority”. Furthermore, on 12 February 2026, the
consultation on Spatial Development Strategies (SDS) and footprints
was published (separate paper) and the Minister for Devolution
wrote to Chief Executives to say that “the development of SDS
footprints is also an opportunity to agree the shape of devolution
geographies for areas currently without a Strategic
Authority”. Areas in England have been invited to submit an
expression of interest by 20 March 2026.






DECISION:

 

RESOLVED:

 
The
Cabinet accepts, in principle, the Secretary
of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government’s
stated intention to explore designating the Council as a Single
Foundation Strategic Authority, consistent with the request for a
Cornwall only Spatial Development Strategy footprint to ensure
coterminosity between the two.

 





 

Reason for the Decision: 
 
As
contained within the report.
 

Alternative options considered:
 
None
other than contained within the report.
 

Conflicts of interest declared:
 
None.

interest:
 
N/A

1. The Committee, after

with the information contained within the report, strongly
recommend that Cabinet retain the existing taxi zones in Cornwall
having considered that:
 
•??Government best
practice is often designed for urban areas and not always best for
Cornwall given its rural areas;
•??Moving from 6 areas to 1 would have negative impact on most
businesses and the Committee is not convinced de-zoning will offer
increased service to customers; 
•??The Committee acknowledges the consultation outcome with
72% of respondents opposed to the changes, while also acknowledging
this does not constitute a referendum; 
•??The Committee considered there were no compelling reasons
to change to a de-zoned area found from information provided by
peer Councils;
•??The Committee acknowledges the fact that should the area be
de-zoned there is no way to undo/reconsider the de-zoning;
•??The Committee is minded that de-zoning could cause
potential disproportionate impact to vulnerable users and rural
areas.

budget be approved, including the setting of rent and service
charges for 2026-27.






DECISION:

 

RESOLVED:

 
1. 
That authority be delegated to the Strategic
Director for Sustainable Growth and Place, in consultation with the
Section 151 Officer and the Portfolio Holder for Housing, to submit
grant applications for the financial year 2026/27 and approve the
acceptance of grants that are consistent with the delivery of the
Housing Revenue Account Business Plan and provided that such
applications are otherwise consistent with the Financial Regulatory
Framework and that any match funding can be met from within the
approved revenue or capital budget.
 
2. 
That authority be delegated to the Strategic
Director for Sustainable Growth and Place, to authorise: the
purchase of additional new build homes or existing homes within
warranty into the HRA for affordable housing, subject to:

 
a.  completion of satisfactory due diligence including
valuation,
 
b.  consultation with the Monitoring Officer and the
Portfolio Holder for Housing,
 
c.  such acquisitions being limited to a maximum value
of £3m in a single transaction or linked transactions (per
vendor), and not to exceed £3m on any one site.
 
d.  being in accordance with the
code of practice for land and properties and HRA budget.

 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO COUNCIL:

1. 
That the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) Business Plan
and budget for 2026/27, as set out in Appendix 1 to the report, be
approved.
2. 
That both social and affordable dwelling rents for
existing tenants increase by CPI (September 2025) plus 1% for the
2026/27 financial year.
3. 
That both social and affordable dwelling rents for
new tenants on new lets to be charged at formula rents for new
tenants increase by CPI (September 2025) plus 1% for the 2026/27
financial year.
4. 
That Shared Ownership rents rise RPI 0.5% in
accordance with the lease for homes that commenced prior to March
2025 and that Shared Ownership rents increase by January 2026 CPI
+1% in line with the lease for homes that commenced after March
2025.
5. 
That garage rents increase by CPI (September 2025)
plus 1% for the 2026/27 financial year.
6. 
That service charges are set based on actual
charges.

As
contained within the report.

None
other than contained within the report.

None.

content:

Council will deliver on its climate and nature targets through
delivery plans aligned to the Council Priorities Plan and budget

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO COUNCIL:

 

That

2026-2029 (Appendix 1), including the detailed budget proposals for
2026/27, are approved in order to provide the financial resources
that deliver against the Council Priorities Plan with a net General
Budget for 2026/27 of £890.339m to be set, and that the
Cumulative Impact Assessment of these proposals (Appendix 3),
together with the results of the public consultation (Appendix 4)
and the comments of the Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny
Committee, are acknowledged and considered.

 

That
the Council Tax requirement for the Council’s own purposes be
set at £468.800m and it be confirmed that the Cornwall
Council element of the Council Tax be increased by 2.99%, plus a
levy of 2% to be spent solely on Adult Social Care, for the
financial year 2026/27 (an overall increase of 4.99%, equivalent to
a Band D charge of £2,086.36).

 
 

That
the Annual Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, as set out in
Appendix 5 to the report, be approved including:

 
 
i. 
The Prudential Indicators and Treasury
Indicators
 
ii. 
The Annual Investment Strategy
 
iii. 
The Minimum Revenue Provision Policy
 

That
the Capital and Investment Strategy, as set out in Appendix 6 to
the report, be approved.

 

That
the revised Capital Programme, as detailed within the report, is
approved.

 

That
the Tamar Bridge & Torpoint Ferry Joint Committee 2026/27
Revenue Budget and Capital Programme and the 2026/27 draft Business
Plan, as referenced in section 4, are approved.

the Deputy Leader be authorised to adjust the recommendations to
Full Council, in consultation with the Section 151 Officer, upon
receipt of additional information following the Final Local
Government Finance Settlement from Government or any further
movement in the 2025/26 financial position, which may change some
assumptions and therefore figures.

 

That
receipt of the grants, as set out in Appendix 7 to the report, and
expenditure in accordance with the terms and conditions of the

Section 151 Officer, in consultation with the Deputy Leader,
subject to compliance with relevant procedural
requirements.

decision_maker: Cornwall Council
content:
It was moved by Councillor
Cole, seconded by Councillor Rowse and
 
RESOLVED that:
 
1. Council Procedure Rule 12.4
be amended as follows to enable more motions to be debated at
Council meetings:-

Motions for which notice has been duly given (other than motions
under Rule 13), shall be debated at the meeting on the basis of the
following:-

(i) Motions approved at Council
relating to an executive function will be advisory and not bind the
Cabinet, or individual Cabinet Member, but may inform their future
decisions.
(ii) Advisory motions relating
to non-executive functions may be considered and approved at
Council or referred to the relevant Committee for detailed
consideration. In the case of the latter, an advisory motion
approved at Council will not bind the future deliberations of the
Committee which the matter has been referred to but may inform its
future recommendations.

Should a motion not be dealt with at a Council meeting for any
reason (other than withdrawal by the proposer), it shall stand
referred by the Chairman to the Cabinet or relevant
Committee.
 
2. As a consequence of (1),
Council Procedure Rule 12.5 be amended as follows:

Where the Council votes on a
motion in an advisory capacity, the Cabinet, individual Cabinet
Member or Committee must report back to the Council within six
months of the date of the Council voting on the motion. Where the
motion relates to an executive function, the Cabinet, or individual
Cabinet Member, shall consider and make a decision on the motion,
and the Leader will report that decision back to Council through
their Leader’s announcements.
 
3. The following parameters be
put in place to support effective agenda management:

(i) The meeting be closed at 6.00pm;
(ii) That the first business on
the agenda should consist of statutory business as set out in
Article 4 of the Constitution;
(iii) That up to three hours be
set aside for motions, and that any motions not discussed be
referred to the relevant body;
(iv) That the Chairman has
discretion to order the motions on the agenda, in consultation with
Group Leaders.
 
ACTION:-

(i) Constitution to be updated accordingly
(ii) Motion template to be
updated and circulated to Members to reflect the above
decision.
topline: The Cornwall Council has decided to amend Council Procedure Rules to allow for more motions to be debated and reported back on within six months.

Mustoe, seconded by Councillor Alvey and
 
RESOLVED
 
1. That this Council mandates
the Leader to write to the Chancellor to point out the devastating
impact her measures, announced in the Autumn Budget 2025, will have
on Cornwall’s Retail, Hospitality and Leisure (RHL)
sector.
2. That this Council opposes
specific measures in the Autumn Budget 2025, which relate to RHL
businesses in Cornwall, and requests the Government to:
(a) Reverse its decision to end existing Retail, Hospitality and
Leisure (RHL) business rates relief (40% up to a cash cap per
business) on 31 March 2026. The consequence of the current policy
will mean that many businesses will face higher bills.
(b) Consider increasing the
business rates discount for hospitality to the full 20p permitted
in legislation.
(c) Commit to delaying business
rates revaluation levels for hospitality businesses and freeze them
at 2023 levels.
(d) Acknowledge that whilst the
Government has introduced lower business rates multipliers for RHL
properties, this is a significantly less generous policy that the
previous 40% relief for many businesses.
(e) Accept that a Transition
Relief Scheme only applies to a limited number of businesses and
slows the increase rather than reducing the overall tax burden RHL
businesses will face.
(f) Implement a 5% reduction in
VAT on Retail, Hospitality and Leisure Businesses.
3. That this Council recognises
the significant social, economic and cultural contribution that
Retail, Hospitality and Leisure businesses provide in Cornwall,
including:
(a) 49,200 job and career
opportunities in the RHL sector in Cornwall alone. (b) RHL GVA in
Cornwall totals £1.35 billion annually – highlighting
this sector as a significant economic driver locally.
4. That this Council urgently
takes action to review the measures announced in the Autumn Budget
2025, provides an assessment on their likely impact on the Retail,
Hospitality and Leisure sector.
5. That this Council provides
and publishes clear guidance on its website on how businesses
affected can mitigate these measures and be supported during this
difficult time.
6. That officers do not take
any action on this decision until Government confirms its
position.
topline: The Cornwall Council has decided to oppose measures in the Autumn Budget 2025 that will negatively impact the Retail, Hospitality, and Leisure sector in Cornwall.

decision_maker: Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Leadership Board
content:
Attendees were welcomed to the
site and enthusiasm was expressed for geothermal energy and its
potential for Cornwall. Eden’s geothermal facilities were
highlighted and it was noted that the meeting room was powered by
geothermal heat and that the nearby horticultural nursery also
benefitted from the system. Representatives from Eden stated that
it considered geothermal a model for how Cornwall could use
technology in the future.
 
The Strategic Director for
Sustainable Growth & Place at Cornwall Council reflected on
Cornwall’s leading role in renewable energy and the
opportunities it created for economic growth, jobs, and supporting
the UK’s wider energy needs. Emphasis was made on turning
geothermal innovation into a full industry for Cornwall, working
alongside partners such as Eden, GEL, Celtic Sea Power and
others. 
 
The Board noted that geothermal
energy was part of the Local Area Energy Plan, which had been
developed over several years with significant public engagement.
The plan included an ambition for around 200 MW of geothermal
power, reflecting strong local support, alignment with
Cornwall’s mining heritage, a low environmental footprint and
the ability to provide reliable baseload energy. It was  noted that geothermal also offered cost advantages
compared with small modular nuclear reactors. 
 
Technical experts explained
different geothermal technologies, from shallow heat systems to
deep geothermal electricity projects like those in Cornwall and the
Board noted that recent technological advances (particularly in
drilling speeds and equipment) have rapidly reduced costs and
improved output, making geothermal far more commercially
viable.
 
Cornwall’s existing
projects, including Eden’s heat system and the United Downs
power project, were presented as evidence of regional leadership
and European and Council investment in these initiatives had
already generated local economic benefits, skills development and
education opportunities, and potential lithium
extraction.
 
Finally, significant
improvements were highlighted including those emerging from the US
FORGE geothermal research programme, which had driven major
advances in drilling performance and had sparked commercial
projects abroad. These developments strengthened the case for
expanding geothermal in the UK and increasing Cornwall’s
contribution beyond the existing 200 MW target.
topline: The Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Leadership Board has decided to approve recommendations for the development of geothermal energy in Cornwall.

decision_maker: Sustainable Growth and Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee,
purpose:
The review of the public subsidised bus
contract in 2028 is a critical moment of this Council
administration. There are a number of options to the role of the
Council, together with the bus industry. Consideration about what
the Council can afford and our priorities of those routes that
should be subsidised is critical for our communities. We will want
to consider this in the context of alternative and complementary
community transport options.
content:
The Head of Strategic Transport
introduced the report (previously circulated) which included a
PowerPoint presentation on Cornwall’s Local Bus
Services  with a particular focus on
2028 when the new contract would be introduced and the Franchising
and Bus Reform Pilot:  In summary
the presentation comprised an overview of the following:
 
· 
Cornwall’s Bus Network.
· 
Challenges.
· 
Considering the future.
· 
Department of Transport Franchising and Bus Reform
Pilot.
· 
2028 Local Bus Contract.
· 
Bus Contract and Bus Reform Governance
Timeline.
· 
Bus franchising – what is it?
· 
Differences between bus network delivery
models.
· 
Delivery models being considered (baseline existing
EP).
· 
Pilot study workstreams.
· 
Workstream activities.
 
During discussions there were a
number of key points raised, including:
 
(i) 
What was
franchising in the context of bus reform?  In response, it was noted that franchising
involved the local authority taking greater control of the bus
network, fares, and operations, requiring increased resources and
responsibility. It was often compared to London-style transport,
though rural areas would not reach those service levels.
(ii) 
Clarification on the
models being considered in the pilot? 
It was noted that this would be an Enhanced Partnership Plus
(building on current arrangements) with 3 franchising
options:
- 
Franchise
supported (contracted) services only.
- 
Franchise
commercial services to align with contracted ones.
- 
Shared
responsibility model with operators (similar to Jersey).
(iii) 
Clarification on the
purpose of the pilot?  In response, it
was noted that it would evaluate the pros and cons, costs,
benefits, and risks of different models, supported by financial and
economic modelling. This would then inform Cornwall Council’s
future approach and provide learning to the Department for
Transport.
(iv) 
Clarification on the
current workstreams.  It was  noted that this included data collection from
operators, public engagement and immersive research with protected
groups, bus operator forum and stakeholder engagement, resourcing
and infrastructure planning (e.g., depots), soft market testing for
external operator interest and financial and economic
modelling
(v) 
Clarification on next
steps?  It was noted that work
would continue until April, then the Council would determine
whether to proceed with contract re-procurement for 2028 or move
toward franchising.
(vi) 
A member
stated that the statement in the presentation suggesting all
communities with a bus service would be retained was not entirely
accurate.
(vii) 
Clarification on if
Cornwall Council adopted a franchise model, how many additional
staff would be required and what the cost would be?  It was noted that an assessment would be carried
out during the pilot period, with findings expected by April.
Staffing needs would depend on the level of control, including
planning the network, fare management, and monitoring standards.
 It was noted that costs could not be
confirmed at this stage but would be considered as part of the
assessment.
(viii) 
Following
a question, the Committee noted that the pilot was fully
funded.
(ix) 
Clarification on the
risks franchising posed compared to the Enhanced Partnership (EP)
model?  It was noted that the main
consideration was the level of control. Under franchising, the
local authority gained full control over the network, which
differed from the EP model.
(x) 
Whether
franchising would limit the ability to use hybrid models or
creative approaches, such as community bus routes?  In response the Committee noted that it would not
and that franchising allowed flexibility and opportunities to
involve community transport. Existing community transport groups
were being engaged through the Bus Operator Forum, and a separate
workstream would focus on community transport opportunities under
both EP and franchising models. There may also be scope for support
from the commercial sector.
(xi) 
Clarification as to
whether local bus services were a statutory requirement or a
business? It was noted that local bus services operated on a
commercial business, but the local authority had statutory
obligations to support the network.
(xii) 
Clarification as to
the main challenge for bus operators? 
It was noted that customer demand was inconsistent, making it
difficult to run a business model.
(xiii) 
Clarification as to
the main complaints about bus services. 
In response it was noted that complaints varied; in rural areas,
the main issue was a lack of regular services, fare increases also
generated concern especially as subsidies from the pilot scheme
ended.
(xiv) 
Whether
bus services should be free?  In
response it was noted that it would require significant investment
and policy decisions at local and national level.  It was, however, noted that some free travel
schemes already existed, such as concessionary passes.
(xv) 
Clarification as to
whether Cornwall Council would always need to subsidise bus
services?  It was noted that due
to Cornwall’s rural nature and long distances, services would
never be fully commercially viable.
(xvi) 
Clarification was
sought on the cost of the current contract? It was noted that it
was currently £12.5 million annually plus inflationary
uplifts, supporting over 50% of the network.  Cornwall supported the third-highest percentage of
bus mileage in England.
(xvii) 
Clarification as to
how Cornwall compared to other rural authorities?  In response it was noted that Cornwall supported
more actual bus mileage than many others, but benchmarking data
would be shared separately.
(xviii) 
Clarification on what
a new contract cost if tendered today would cost, it was noted that
it would likely be significantly more than £12.5
million.
(xix) 
Clarification on the
funding Cornwall was receiving from government?  In response it was noted that it was £6.78
million per year from 2026–27 to 2028–29 (total
£20.35 million). However, this was cash-flat and would reduce
in real terms due to inflation.
(xx) 
Explanation
of  the regulatory framework for bus
services?  The current deregulated
framework was introduced in 1985 and implemented in 1986. Bus
operators decide routes, timetables, and fares. Local authorities
identify gaps in service (e.g., evenings, Sundays) and procure
contracts to fill them. Over time, government funding has
decreased, leading to more local authority involvement through Bus
Service Improvement Plans and options like franchising for greater
control.
(xxi) 
Clarification as to
what is franchising was and where it was being adopted?  The Committee noted that franchising gave local
authorities full control over the network, similar to
London’s model. It was mainly being adopted in large urban
areas (e.g., Manchester, Liverpool) where services were more
commercially viable. Local authorities could choose between
franchising or maintaining a deregulated model with enhanced
partnerships.
(xxii) 
Clarification on the
funding for the bus network? It was noted that funding came from
multiple sources, including Central Government grants to local
authorities, local authority budgets for contracted services,
concessionary travel reimbursement from a separate budget and bus
service operators grant (fuel duty rebate).  It was noted that many people still assumed
councils ran bus services, which had not been the case for 40
years.
(xxiii) 
Whether
Cornwall would always need to subsidise bus services?  In response it was noted that due to
Cornwall’s rural nature and long distances, services would
never be fully commercially viable.
(xxiv) 
Clarification on the
additional powers a Mayoral authority would have over the bus
network? In response it was noted that mayoral authorities
typically gained greater powers over transport, including
franchising.  Further clarification was
sought on whether Cornwall, as a foundational strategic authority,
would miss out on powers available to combined mayoral authorities
under the English Devolution Bill.
(xxv) 
Whether
smaller buses or minibuses could be used instead of large buses on
narrow rural lanes?  In reply officers
advised that operators would need two fleets, doubling capital
costs. Fuel and driver costs remained the same while vehicles were
on the road. Most buses are tied into the school transport network,
making fleet changes impractical. The focus should be on increasing
passenger numbers to avoid empty buses.
(xxvi) 
Whether
community transport was part of the solution?  It was noted that  community transport would be part of the mix, but
it differed from smaller hopper buses operated by commercial
providers. Staffing was also a challenge, as drivers often required
full-time work, not split shifts.
(xxvii) 
How
housing development assumptions affected bus planning?  It was noted that transport strategies aligned
with housing strategies set by government targets.  The Committee noted the importance of linking with
the Local Plan.
(xxviii)Whether data on free
travel and demographics was available, it was noted that data was
collected and published by the Department for Transport. Officers
could provide specific data on request but aimed to avoid
overloading the Committee with unnecessary information.
(xxix) 
Confirmation as to
whether the Transport Strategy was considering buses and rail
together, including projects like Mid Cornwall Metro?  In response it was noted that the strategy aimed
to provide an integrated public transport network, including buses,
rail, cycling, and walking. Cornwall’s Local Transport Plan
(to 2030) set this out, and government guidance on future plans was
expected soon. Integration of timetables and ticketing was a key
goal.
(xxx) 
Whether
improving rail services impacted bus usage?  In response, it was noted that improvements to
rail increased rail patronage, not bus usage directly. Rail and bus
services were reviewed together to ensure connectivity, as rail was
less flexible and more expensive to expand, while buses offered
flexibility.
(xxxi) 
Clarification as to
whether commercial operators like First Bus withdraw services
without penalty?  Officers advised that
under the current deregulated model, operators can withdraw
services without contractual penalties if they are not receiving
local authority funding and within the spirit of the Enhanced
Partnership, which was a voluntary agreement.
(xxxii) 
Whether
future models included penalties or contractual obligations to
prevent operators from withdrawing services?  It was noted that under franchising or joint
venture models, operators would be contractually bound, reducing
the risk of withdrawal. Franchising gave full control to the
authority, while joint ventures retained some operator flexibility
within a contractual framework.
(xxxiii)Clarification on the
difference between Enhanced Partnership, Enhanced Partnership Plus,
and franchising?  It was noted that
Enhanced Partnership: Voluntary collaboration with agreed
conditions (e.g., limiting service changes). Enhanced Partnership
Plus: Similar but with greater shared responsibility. Franchising:
Full contractual control by the authority; operators deliver
services to authority standards.  Joint
Venture: A hybrid model combining contractual obligations with some
operator flexibility and incentives.
(xxxiv) 
Whether
franchising would shorten procurement times compared to current
contracts?  Officers advised that
procurement under franchising still took time, but contracts
typically lasted 5–6 years (sometimes up to 8 years).
Franchising could involve multiple smaller contracts to include
small and medium operators.
(xxxv) 
Whether
future plans would improve flexibility and affordability of bus
services for students in Further Education given current funding
pressures on colleges?  In response, it
was noted that currently, the Council had statutory obligations for
home-to-school transport, while post-16 transport was managed by
colleges using local bus networks. Under future models being
considered, the Council could take greater control, which may allow
improvements. However, greater control brought increased costs and
risks, and these would need to be assessed as part of ongoing
work
(xxxvi) 
Whether
there were measures to ensure affordable bus routes for people who
relied on buses to get to work?  It was
noted that the Council was working to understand travel patterns
and improve provision where possible. Current incentives included
low fares and schemes introduced during the Bus Fare Pilot. Data
from operators was helping identify gaps and plan socially
necessary services where commercial routes were not
viable
(xxxvii) 
Whether
there was a strategy to move passengers from buses to
trains?  Officers advised that the
strategy was to create a comprehensive public transport network
offering choice. Rail acts as a backbone, with buses providing
connections, supported by walking, cycling, and micro-mobility. The
aim was integration, not shifting passengers away from
buses.
(xxxviii) 
Whether
future contracts would ensure connectivity to key destinations,
such as Derriford Hospital from Liskeard?  Officers confirmed that connecting communities to
essential destinations remained a priority and that discussions
would continue with local Community Area Partnerships (CAPs) groups
to explore options, including potential pilot schemes for direct
services.
 
Following consideration of the
report and extensive debate it was 
moved by Councillor Donnithorne, seconded by Councillor Mitchell
and
 
RESOLVED
that
 
1. 
The
Cabinet Member for Transport be recommended  to endorse the progression of the reported
workstream as set out in the report to inform the local bus network
contract arrangements and take note of the comments made by the
Strategic Growth and Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee (as set
out in the minutes).
2. 
The
Committee be presented with a formal Options report for
consideration by the Overview and Scrutiny Committee in advance of
any decision being made by Cabinet.
topline: The Sustainable Growth and Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee has recommended endorsing the progression of workstreams to inform local bus network contract arrangements in Cornwall.

content:
Questions were put to
the Cabinet Member for Transport as follows:
 
1. 
Clarification on the
proposals for overnight camping in Cornwall Council car
parks?  The Cabinet Member advised that
the proposal would allow self-contained motorhomes to camp
overnight in about 12 car parks and clarification would be sought
on conditions.
2. 
Clarification as to
the interest in providing longer-term van dwelling
sites?  In response the Cabinet Member
advised that discussions were taking place to consider potential
sites for longer stays as housing solutions and income
generation.
3. 
Clarification as to
when public consultation would commence on the “Off Street
Parking Order”.  The Cabinet
Member stated that it would start this week and would be followed
by statutory car parking notice requirements and publicised via the
Council website and media channels.
 
Questions were put to
the Cabinet Member for Tourism, Localism and Planning as
follows:
 
4. 
Clarification as to
who was funding the Global Cornish launch event and the
cost?  The Cabinet Member stated that
the aim was to encourage inward investment for Cornwall and that
costs and Council contribution would be shared with the
Committee.
5. 
Clarification on what
was happening with Visit Cornwall and the tourism
marketing?  The Cabinet Member reminded
the Committee Visit Cornwall had gone into liquidation and that the
Council was safeguarding assets (website, brand) and funding
short-term marketing until March 2026. 
It was noted that a sector summit was scheduled for 27 January at
Eden to plan future governance and strategy.
 
Questions were put to
the Cabinet Member for Economic, Regeneration and Investment as
follows:
 
6. 
Clarification on the
outlook for Cornwall’s minerals strategy and lithium
jobs?  The Cabinet Member advised that
jobs already existed in lithium and tin and that the Government was
investing significantly in Cornish Lithium which would create more
high-paid jobs, but timelines were unclear. It was noted that
figures could be provided upon request.
7. 
Clarification if/how
the  Council could help businesses
facing business rate hikes?  In response
the Cabinet Member stated that business rates were set by
Government and that the Council could not change rates but did
offer discretionary reliefs.  It was
noted that concerns would be communicated to government.
 
Questions were put to the
Cabinet Member for Housing as follows:
 
8. 
Was a
£24M investment over four years enough for housing
improvements?  The Cabinet Member stated
that it was a good start but agreed it was not enough. He advised
that an additional £10m per year was planned, totalling
£40m over four years in order  to
address damp, mould, and decency issues.
9. 
Clarification was to
whether affordable housing targets could be maintained despite
viability challenges?  The Cabinet
Member stated that the Council was legally bound to consider
viability assessments, which could reduce affordable housing
delivery. It was noted that work with Homes England for extra
funding was ongoing.
10. 
Clarification was
sought as to how a stagnating housing market was being considered
in future strategy?  The Cabinet Member
acknowledged that open market sales were slowing nationally and
that the Council remained focussed on affordable housing delivery
and Homes England support.
 
Questions were put to
the Cabinet Member for Environment & Climate Change as
follows:
 
11. 
Whether
specific car parks or street lighting issues could be reviewed? The
Committee noted specific street lighting issues being experienced
at Torpoint. The Cabinet Member stated that Councillors could
submit issues on a case by case basis.
topline: The Sustainable Growth and Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations on overnight camping, van dwelling sites, public consultation on parking orders, tourism funding, housing improvements, and environmental issues.

decision_maker: Constitution and Governance Committee
content:
It was moved by
Councillor Rowse, seconded by Councillor Chopak, and
 
RESOLVED 
that it be RECOMMENDED TO COUNCIL that:
 
1. 
Council
Procedure Rule 12.4 be amended as follows to enable more motions to
be debated at Council meetings:-
 
Motions for which notice has been duly given (other than motions
under Rule 13), shall be debated at the meeting on the basis of the
following:-
 
(i) 
Motions
approved at Council relating to an executive function will be
advisory and not bind the Cabinet, or individual Cabinet Member,
but may inform their future decisions.
(ii) 
Advisory motions
relating to non-executive functions may be considered and approved
at Council or referred to the relevant Committee for detailed
consideration.  In the case of the
latter, an advisory motion approved at Council will not bind the
future deliberations of the Committee which the matter has been
referred to but may inform its future
recommendations.
 
Should a motion not be dealt with at a Council meeting for any
reason (other than withdrawal by the proposer), it shall stand
referred by the Chairman to the Cabinet or relevant
Committee.
 
2. 
As a
consequence of (1), Council Procedure Rule 12.5 be amended as
follows:
 
Where the Council votes on a
motion in an advisory capacity, the Cabinet, individual Cabinet
Member or Committee must report back to the Council within six
months of the date of the Council voting on the motion. Where the
motion relates to an executive function, the Cabinet, or individual
Cabinet Member, shall consider and make a decision on the motion,
and the Leader will report that decision back to Council through
their Leader’s announcements.
 
It was further recommended by
Cole, seconded by Councillor Rowse, that:-
 
1. 
It be
recommended to Council that the following parameters be put in
place to support effective agenda management:
 
 
i. 
The
meeting be closed at 6.00pm;
 
ii. 
That the
first business on the agenda should consist of statutory business
as set out in Article 4 of the Constitution;
 
iii. 
That up to
three hours be set aside for motions, and that any motions not
discussed be referred to the relevant body;
 
iv. 
That the
Chairman has discretion to order the motions on the agenda, in
consultation with Group Leaders.
 
It was further RESOLVED
that:
 
2. 
Authority
be delegated to the Monitoring Officer, in consultation with the
Chairman and Vice-Chairman of this Committee, to draft appropriate
wording to support the constitutional position for inclusion in the
report to Council with the Committee’s
recommendation.
 
3.   A placeholder
be made on this Committee’s work programme to enable a review
of any changes approved by Council, after twelve months of
operation, should this prove necessary.
topline: The Constitution and Governance Committee has decided to amend Council Procedure Rules to allow for more motions to be debated at Council meetings.

The

include a reflection on progress to date now that the CPO has been

financing expectations for the next 4 years and beyond. The second

decision_maker: Cornwall Council
content:
It was moved by Councillor
Cole, seconded by Councillor Rowse and
 
RESOLVED
that Procedure Rule 4.2.2 be amended, as
follows:

Where a Member of a committee is unable
to attend a meeting, they have the following options:
1. The Member may arrange for a
validated substitute to attend from their group, and not take part
in the meeting (save where this is expressly excluded in the
constitution);
2. The Member may join remotely
in a non-voting capacity to speak, and
not appoint a substitute.
 
If a substitute Member is
appointed, the substantive Member may not attend the meeting. This
does not prevent the substantive Member from watching the matter on
livestream or similar.
 
The first of either the
substantive Member or the validated substitute to join the meeting
will be judged to be the Member formally participating for the
duration of the meeting. Where the substitute is the participating
Member and the substantive Member seeks to join remotely, the
Chairman of the meeting will exclude the latter from the remainder
of the meeting.
 
ACTION: Constitution to be
updated accordingly.
topline: The Cornwall Council has decided to amend Procedure Rule 4.2.2 regarding member attendance and participation in meetings.

decision_maker: Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Leadership Board
content:
Matt Barton, Service Director
for Strategy and Partnerships, deputised for the Chief Executive
and provided an update from the Executive Group. He noted that
several issues discussed at the October meeting were now appearing
on the current agenda, which demonstrated the value of the
Executive Group in reviewing draft reports before they came to the
Leadership Board for consideration.
 
He highlighted that Chris
Parsons from MHCLG had updated the group on the new Secretary of
State’s commitment to fairer funding for local authorities.
This was particularly relevant as the Government had since
published the Local Government Finance Policy Statement, setting
out a new funding formula for the next three years. Matt advised
that it was too early to determine the impact on the
Council’s finances. He also referred to the English
Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill (the Bill), which at the
time was progressing through the Bill Committee. The Council was
among 52 organisations that submitted evidence, and the Bill had
since reached report stage before returning to the House of
Commons. Matt noted that its implications for Cornwall remained
significant and invited Perran Moon MP to comment further on the
Bill’s progress and potential impact.
 
Perran Moon MP then provided an
update on fair funding and devolution. He noted that, although
detailed analysis was still required, the fair funding review
appeared likely to place Cornwall in a worse position rather than
improve it. He expressed hope that the forthcoming budget might
include positive announcements for Cornwall, potentially linked to
the Bill, and acknowledged the efforts of Cornwall’s MPs in
advocating for the area.  Perran
confirmed that significant detail remained unknown and that a
four-week consultation with MPs would precede official
announcements before Christmas. On devolution, he reported that the
Bill had passed through the Bill Committee without major changes
and was now at report stage in the House of Commons, scheduled for
debate the following week. He advised that several amendments,
including one relating specifically to Cornish devolution, had been
tabled, and the Bill would subsequently progress to the Lords for
further scrutiny. The Leader thanked Perran for his work on both
fair funding and devolution.
topline: The Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Leadership Board has decided to approve recommendations regarding fair funding and devolution, with potential impacts on Cornwall's finances and governance.

decision_maker: Committee in Common between Cornwall Health and Wellbeing Board and the Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Integrated Care Partnership
content:
The Chief Finance Officer of
the ICB informed the Committee that the organisation had been
working towards a significant restructure aimed at achieving
approximately 50% reduction in staffing costs across the ICB
through clustering by the end of March 2026.  It was noted that consultation on the full
organisational change was expected to commence in early January,
with a separate consultation regarding the executive structure
anticipated in December, subject to confirmation with the NHS
Executive.  It was noted that the scale
of the change was significant and the organisation continued to
work on delivering in-year operational targets for 2025/26 whilst
also planning for 2026/27 and support was being provided to Devon
to help improve its position for 2026/27.  He stated that further details regarding the
consultation process would be confirmed following the ICB Board
meeting on the 27 November whereupon, engagement with staff and
colleagues would begin to manage the change process.
 
The Deputy Chair of Cornwall
ICB reported that performance in Cornwall had remained positive
with trusts performing well in national league tables. Winter
pressures, including COVID, flu, and emergency admissions were
noted as ongoing challenges but despite this, Cornwall was entering
the planning round for the next year in a relatively strong
position compared to other areas.
 
The Service Director for
Strategy and Partnerships provided an update on the significant
financial challenges for Cornwall Council stating that there was a
projected budget gap of £45–70 million for the
forthcoming financial year. It was noted that to address this, a
comprehensive spending review had been initiated by Cabinet and
referred to the development of the Council Priorities Plan for the
next four years which had been approved for consultation and the
formulation of a three-year budget shaped by the priorities. He
advised that the exact budget gap was expected to be clarified
following the Government’s finance policy statement and the
Chancellor’s Autumn Statement and budget consultation was
scheduled for December and January.  He
then referred to the upcoming Local Government Association
corporate peer challenge commencing 12 January and a  sector-led review would assess Council performance
across five themes and advised that the Committee was invited to
meet the review team during its visit.
topline: The Committee in Common between Cornwall Health and Wellbeing Board and the Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Integrated Care Partnership has decided to approve recommendations for significant restructuring and cost reduction plans.

strategic direction for the integrated commissioning of voluntary

an admission to hospital or adult social care service and to
support safe and timely discharges from hospital. It will set out a
programme of transformational commissioning in the context of the
statutory requirements and good practice guidance.

1. 
That the Home Based Prevention and Intermediate Care
Business Case, as set out in Appendix 1 and exempt Appendix 2 to

Integrated Commissioning of Home Based Intermediate Care and
includes the Council assuming the lead commissioning role for

proceed on the basis of the Council contingency
approach.  This includes the Council
assuming the commissioning role for the Council funded services
only, including those in Service Areas 3 (Corserv IDA only) and
5.

be delegated to the Strategic Director for Safe and Caring

Social Care and Health Partnerships, including any final amendments

Partnerships.

decision_maker: Cabinet
content:
The
Leader started his announcements with the positive news about
Cornwall Airport Newquay and Cornwall’s wider connectivity,
with the Cornwall to London Public Service Obligation route being a
vital link for residents and businesses.  The Leader was pleased to confirm that an interim
provider was in place to maintain flights between Newquay and
Gatwick and that, following the collapse of Eastern Airways,
officers had worked flat out to restore the service and ensure the
essential route remained up and running with daily flights resuming
from 23 November 2025, rising to twice daily from mid-February
2026. 
 
The
Leader felt that it was important to note that the decision was
separate from the full Public Service Obligation tender process,
which was still in progress and he thanked everyone involved for
moving so quickly and helping keep Cornwall connected.
 
Turning
to how Cornwall was helping to lead nationally on health and work,
the Leader was pleased that the Council had been named as one of
the employer-led Vanguards supporting Sir Charlie Mayfield’s
Keep Britain Working review and was the only non-mayoral authority
that had been chosen.  The three-year
partnership with the Government would help employers test practical
approaches to prevent ill health, support people to stay in work
and build healthier, more resilient workplaces.  The Leader stated it was an opportunity to show
that business-led ideas worked in rural and coastal areas like
Cornwall, not just big cities and, more importantly, that it
recognised the leadership many Cornish employers already showed
when it came to health and wellbeing at work.
 
Cornwall had also lead the way nationally in respect of its
successes with Transport for Cornwall and the Leader was pleased
that the Council had been selected by the Government to take part
in a pilot scheme looking at how local authorities could run and
support their bus services.  The
findings would help the Government shape bus services for other
rural local authorities in the future.
 
Finally, the Leader stated that three upcoming Westminster
engagements underlined how active the Cabinet was in making
Cornwall’s case on the national stage.  The Portfolio Holder for Community Safety and
Public Health, the Director of Public Health and Exeter University
would soon be presenting the Pretty Poverty report to the
Government that highlighted hidden rural poverty and argued for
fairer funding and targeted support in Cornwall. 
 
The
Portfolio Holder for Housing would soon been meeting Homes England
to progress a Homes Cornwall and Homes
England pilot, with the aim of unlocking affordable homes for local
people and speeding up delivery through a stronger partnership and
the Deputy Leader and Portfolio Holder for Reswources would soon be
attending the Global Cornish launch event, hosted by Perran Moon MP
that aimed to mobilise Cornwall’s diaspora and encourage
investment back into Cornwall. 
 
Taken
together, those engagements showed a Cabinet that was deeply
invested in protecting essential services, improving health and
work outcomes and championing Cornwall at home and
abroad.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations for maintaining flights, advancing health and work initiatives, and participating in a pilot scheme for bus services in Cornwall.

decision_maker: Sustainable Growth and Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Questions were put to the
Cabinet Member for Economic, Regeneration and Investment as
follows:
 
1. 
How would Cornwall ensure that South East Cornish
residents and suppliers benefited from the Devonport investment
programme, rather than being priced out or burdened by tolls and
transport costs?  In response it was
noted that approximately 25% of Devonport’s current workforce
already lived in Cornwall.  It was
further noted that the Council aimed to secure well-paid jobs for
Cornish residents and avoid importing workers from outside Devon
and Cornwall.  The Cabinet Member
advised that plans included improving transport links (Torpoint
Ferry, train services) and creating new homes within commuting
distance.  He referred to the MOU signed
with Devon partners to ensure regional collaboration and
highlighted the importance of skills development making reference
to Falmouth Docks and how it could play a role in supporting naval
operations during Devonport’s transition.
2. 
Clarification was sought as to whether Westminster
was acknowledging Cornwall’s economic challenges and whether
Cornwall’s MPs were supporting the case?  In response, it was noted that progress had
improved recently and that MPs were actively lobbying
Government.  The Cabinet Member advised
that a major housing meeting was scheduled in Westminster next week
to push for a housing deal for Cornwall with an aim of securing
funding without requiring a mayoral system.  It was recognised that the ending of the Shared
Prosperity Fund was of concern, but there was hope for alternative
funding  such as Evergreen repayable
grants.  The Cabinet Member referred to
positive signals from the Environment Secretary which suggested
places would not need mayoral status to access funds.  It was noted that there was expectations of some
funding but unfortunately it would not be at the level previously
available under EU schemes.
3. 
Clarification was requested as to whether County
Farms were being sold off?  In response,
the Cabinet Member stated that County Farms were not being sold and
that decisions related only to selling farmhouses and small parcels
of land where tenancies had ended or the tenant had left. It was
noted that this was routine estate management. 
4. 
Clarification was sought as to why farmhouses and
land were being sold.  In response the
Committee noted that it was to manage the estate effectively,
balance revenue, and de-risk the capital programme.  Funds raised would help maintain and improve the
10,500 acre farm estate and support housing priorities for Cornish
residents.
5. 
Confirmation as to how much money sales would
raise?  The Cabinet Member stated
that approximately £2 million from previous similar sales had
been raised and exact figures for the current and future sales
(including the 11 farms mentioned for 2026) could be provided by
relevant officers.
6. 
Clarification as to whether capital receipts would
be ring-fenced for farms?  It was noted
that they would not and that Cornwall Council’s policy was
for capital receipts to go into the general pot. However, it was
noted that Cabinet had allocated around £16 million to the
farm estate from overall funds.
7. 
Clarification as to the long-term commitment to the
farm estate?  The Cabinet Member advised
that Cabinet was committed to retaining and improving the farm
estate. It was noted that over 96% remained farmland and that there
were no plans to introduce technology (e.g., satellite analysis for
crop optimization) but to support community initiatives like
allotments.
8. 
Clarification on media reports that suggested farms
were being sold off?  It was noted that
these reports were incorrect and misleading and that the Council
was not selling farms wholesale; only farmhouses and small parcels
of land.
9. 
Confirmation as to how South East Cornwall would be
involved in the Devonport Growth Area? The Cabinet Member
acknowledged the importance of collaboration and noted that housing
and transport issues would be addressed.  It was noted that South East Cornwall was
ready to contribute with housing, business sites, and
infrastructure improvements.
 
Questions were put to
the Cabinet Member for Housing as follows:
 
1. Clarification as to
the steps Cornwall Council had taken to prevent or mitigate the
removal of outdoor bins by Cornwall Housing?  The Cabinet Member explained that Cornwall Housing
Limited was in a precarious financial position and needed to invest
every penny into upgrading council housing stock to meet regulatory
obligations. Non-essential activities, such as maintaining dog bins
had been cut to save money.  The
Cabinet Member advised that Cornwall Housing had consulted with
every town and parish council about taking on the bins which some
had agreed to, whilst others had not. Cornwall Council had no
funding to take these bins on themselves and aimed to educate
residents to dispose of waste responsibly.
2. Explanation as to
why Cornwall Housing was described as failing as a
landlord?  The Cabinet Member confirmed
that there were significant issues with Cornwall Housing meeting
decency standards and stated that it had an 8 year programme to
achieve compliance
3. Clarification as to
the situation with solohaus modular
units and costs?  The Cabinet Member
admitted that deployment costs of solohaus were “eye-watering” and
unsustainable and therefore a decision had been taken to stop
further deployment and allow existing communities to expire
naturally.  It was noted that buying
traditional houses was more cost-effective. 
4. Confirmation as to
whether Cornwall Council could commit to maintaining affordable
housing delivery rates?  The Cabinet
Member  stated that his personal
ambition was to deliver 50% affordable housing across developments
which was challenging for the Council to achieve. 
5. Clarification as to
how Cornwall Council would address development viability and
stalled sites?  The Cabinet Member
acknowledged viability challenges and referred to Government
subsidy from Homes England which was essential in building homes
particularly for small rural sites.  He
welcomed expressions of interest from community-led organizations
and not just large developers.
6. Clarification as to
what was being done about long-term voids in housing
stock?  The Cabinet Member confirmed he
had challenged the housing team to reduce void turnaround times and
a motion to Council was expected at the next meeting to address
this.  Investment plans were being
developed to speed up void turnover.
7.  Clarification on the future of the solohaus stock?  The
Cabinet Member confirmed that un-deployed units would be subject to
open bids and existing communities would be demobilized as planning
permissions expired. It was noted that all solohaus modular units would be phased out due to
their short lifespan (5–10 years).
 
Questions were put to the
Cabinet Member for Tourism, Localism and Planning as
follows:
 
1.   Clarification as to what was the situation
regarding Visit Cornwall’s liquidation and the
Council’s response?  The Cabinet
Member explained that Visit Cornwall had gone into liquidation and
a legal process was underway. She stated that the Council had to
wait for clarity on asset distribution before taking full control.
Meanwhile, she advised the Committee that she had met with key
sector leads, including the former Chair of Visit Cornwall and a
representative from Visit Britain to discuss risks and next steps.
She stated that the Council intended to consult widely across the
sector and gather information through a listening exercise before
moving to a sector forum to agree future arrangements.
2.    Confirmation as to
how the Council was engaging on the Local Plan and reflecting local
communities?  The Cabinet
Member stated that the current phase was informal and was aimed at
shaping the plan by gathering initial insights about each
geographical area. She confirmed that workshops were being held and
feedback collected to inform the formal consultation phase. The
Cabinet Member stated that the Council had promoted sessions via
social media, short films, and media interviews and planned broader
outreach during the formal stage.
3.  Reassurance was sought on how Visit
Cornwall’s website value and search visibility was being
protected? The Cabinet Member acknowledged the website’s
extensive value and confirmed that Cornwall Council was waiting for
the legal process to conclude before taking full control. She noted
that an asset lock had been put in place when Visit Cornwall was
established, which should return assets to the Council. She assured
the Committee that the Council had expertise to maintain and
protect the website’s SEO value and was preparing to act
quickly once assets were secured.
4.  Clarification as to whether the
Council was willing to work with stakeholders to restore membership
and website functionality?  The Cabinet
Member confirmed her willingness to collaborate and emphasised that
quick steps were needed to maintain sector confidence while
awaiting legal clarity.
 
There were no questions for the
Cabinet Member for Transport or Environment and Climate
Change.
topline: The Sustainable Growth and Place Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for the sale of farmhouses and land in Cornwall, while addressing concerns about Cornwall Housing's financial position and outdoor bin maintenance.

decision_maker: Health and Adult Social Care Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
RESOLVED that:
1. 
The Committee receives the recommendations and
accepts the key asks set out within the Healthwatch, Evolving
Voices in Mental Health Cornwall report to:
i. 
Monitor waiting-time reduction as a standing
item.
ii. 
Scrutinise workforce deployment across Primary Care
Networks.
iii. 
Champion local delivery to reduce out-of-county
placements.
iv. 
Ensure lived experience remains a design principle,
not a footnote.
2. 
The Committee recognises that without the
comprehensive changes outlined by the great work of Healthwatch
within its report, the changes discussed would not have been
possible and acknowledge health partners acceptance of the
findings.
3. 
The Committee is assured that the system partners
have been working in response to address the issues and
recommendations made in the report.
4. 
In developing a future mental health strategy for
Cornwall the issues raised in this report are considered while
adopting a whole life course approach to mental health.
5. 
Officers investigate the availability and potential
for mental health training for Members.
topline: The Health and Adult Social Care Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for improving mental health services in Cornwall

decision_maker: Constitution and Governance Committee
content:
It was moved by Councillor
Cole, seconded by Councillor Rowse, and
 
RESOLVED 
that it be RECOMMENDED TO COUNCIL that:
 
1. 
The proposed changes to Article 21 –
Governance Arrangements of Council Owned Entities be implemented
immediately, subject to the inclusion of the amendments as
referenced in the minutes, including:
 
a) 
Revised wording in the protocol regarding the
purpose of the entities;
b) 
Confirmation that both officers and Members may
serve on Boards, with reference to training requirements for all
Board Members (both officer and Member);
c) 
Inclusion of a glossary of key terms;
d) 
Clarification of the role of scrutiny within
paragraphs 7.1 to 7.3;
e) 
A review of the governance arrangements to be
undertaken by the Corporate Finance and Performance Overview and
Scrutiny Committee within 12 to 18 months of Full Council’s
decision, with any issues referred back to the Constitution and
Governance Committee as necessary.
 
 
2. 
Authority be delegated to the Head of Commercial
Assurance to make amendments to the Protocol, including
grammatical, legislative compatibility and other minor amends when
required.
 
It was also moved
that:
 
Subject to Full Council’s
decision on the above recommendations, the proposed changes to the
Protocol for Governance Arrangements of Council Owned Entities be
approved.
topline: The Constitution and Governance Committee has decided to implement changes to the governance arrangements of council owned entities.

decision_maker: Constitution and Governance Committee
content:
It was moved by Councillor
Rowse, seconded by Councillor Kenny, and
 
RESOLVED 
that it be RECOMMENDED TO COUNCIL that Procedure Rule 4.2.2
be amended, as follows:
 
Where a Member of a committee
is unable to attend a meeting, they have the following
options:
 
1. 
The Member may arrange for a validated substitute to
attend from their group, and not take part in the meeting (save
where this is expressly excluded in the constitution);
2. 
The Member may join remotely in a non-voting
capacity to speak, and not appoint a substitute.
 
If a substitute Member is
appointed, the substantive Member may not attend the
meeting.  This does not prevent the
substantive Member from watching the matter on livestream or
similar.
 
The first of either the
substantive Member or the validated substitute to join the meeting
will be judged to be the Member formally participating for the
duration of the meeting.  Where the
substitute is the participating Member and the substantive Member
seeks to join remotely, the Chairman of the meeting will exclude
the latter from the remainder of the meeting.
topline: The Constitution and Governance Committee has decided to amend Procedure Rule 4.2.2 regarding Member attendance at meetings.

decision_maker: Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
It was
moved by Councillor German, seconded by Councillor M Thomas
and
 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO CABINET:
 
1. 
That the
delivery of social housing to increase to the UK average per
100,000 people be prioritised, with the appropriate number of new
homes adapted for disabled people.
 
It was
moved by Councillor German, seconded by Councillor Webb
and
 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO CABINET:
 
2. 
That the
challenges and opportunities of food and energy security be
recognised and that explicit targets be set in those
areas. 
 
It was
moved by Councillor German, seconded by Councillor Ewert
and
 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO CABINET:
 
3. 
That Blue
Light integration be prioritised within Cornwall and that the
Government be asked for the powers to pilot a Blue Light
Integration Model to enhance services to residents and drive
efficiencies in emergency services, building on the success of
TriService.
 
There
was one abstention.
 
It was
moved by Councillor German, seconded by Councillor Alvey
and
 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO CABINET:
 
4. 
That use
of existing legal powers to take action against sewage pollution in
Cornwall’s waterways and seas be prioritised.
 
It was
moved by Councillor Alvey, seconded by Councillor Webb
and
 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO CABINET:
 
5. 
That, in
respect of the “a resilient economy creating good growth and
jobs” priority that the importance of tourism and changing
pattern of tourism in Cornwall be reflected and that the tourism
sector be supported in this important area of the Cornish
economy.
 
It was
moved by Councillor M Thomas, seconded by Councillor Ewert
and
 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO CABINET:
 
6. 
That the
importance of the Corporate Parenting role of all Cornwall Council
Members be prioritised and that efforts be made to increase the
public’s awareness of it. 
 
There
was one vote against the motion.
 
It was
moved by Councillor M Thomas, seconded by Councillor Ewert
and
 

RESOLVED TO RECOMMEND TO CABINET:
 
7. 
That the
importance of dealing with SEND issues in Cornwall be recognised
and, in particular, the challenges faced in Cornwall.
topline: The Budget Development Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to recommend to Cabinet various measures including prioritising social housing, food and energy security, Blue Light integration, sewage pollution action, tourism support, and SEND issues.

decision_maker: Together for Families Overview and Scrutiny Committee
content:
Question from Ms K Williams of
Mevagissey.
 
Can the Transport Policy be
reviewed, St Austell which encompasses both Penrice/Poltair needs
to be a shared designated area. This has been done previously in
Newquay and Penzance. In 2020 & 2024 Children from Mevagissey
weren't granted their designated school due to oversubscription.
Rural communities should have a choice.
 
The Chair responded as
follows:
 
Thank you for your question,
and we appreciate you taking the time to share your concerns
regarding Cornwall Council’s Home to School Travel Assistance
policy and how this affects families in Mevagissey.
 
Cornwall Council is responsible
for implementing and managing this policy, in line with the
requirements set by the Department for Education. While we are
legally obliged to observe the minimum requirements, we hold the
ability to exercise discretion in some areas, such as providing
transport to designated schools. This is above and beyond offering
transport to the “nearest suitable school with room”
that we are legally required to offer.
 
Any reviews or amendments of
any Council policy would need to follow the due democratic process
that mandates that any proposal would include a thorough public
consultation to give affected users across Cornwall  an
opportunity to give their views and suggestions, as well as to
understand the budget implications. Should the Home to School
Travel Assistance be reviewed, the consultation would include not
only families in Mevagissey but families, carers and schools across
Cornwall, to ensure transparency and fairness.
 
Given that this matter would
constitute a “key decision” – those affecting
communities in two or more electoral divisions , following the
public consultation, any final decision would be subject to a
Cabinet discussion, as it holds the responsibility for approving
new policies, make significant changes to existing policies and to
establish the financial impacts.
 
The speaker responded with a
supplementary question, respectfully asking the Committee to
consider that St Austell already had 2 shared designated areas for
primary schools and the bus provided by the Council was a shared
service for both Poltair and Penrice Schools.  She, therefore, asked for her request to be
considered in line with the Council’s aims to become carbon
neutral and common sense principles that it was pushing forward
with.
 
In response the Head of
Connectivity and Transport Policy stated that the Council
appreciated the concerns  raised and
understood the issue had already been through the appeals
process.  She advised that any change to
the current policy must follow the appropriate due process which
included  formal consultation and
decision by Cabinet as there would be budgetary
implications.  The Chair recognised the
wider impact the matter had across Cornwall and would ensure it was
discussed further with the relevant Cabinet Member and would keep
the speaker updated on progress.
topline: The Together for Families Overview and Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations for a review of the Transport Policy in St Austell to address concerns about school allocations in Mevagissey.
